newsitem.title: UK: British minister tries to cheer gloomy colleagues.
newsitem.headline: British minister tries to cheer gloomy colleagues.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke tried on Friday to put new heart into the battered Conservative Party by warning that the country would be fleeing from reality if it elected a Labour government.

With a new poll showing Labour 25 points ahead of the Conservatives with less than seven weeks to go to an expected May 1 election, Conservatives gathered in Bath, western England, for the party's annual Central Council meeting.
Clarke, in an address ahead of the meeting, warned that if Labour won, Britain would turn its back on the liberalising economic approach that he claimed was making it a role model for the world.
And he launched a furious attack on Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown for refusing to be spell out how he would run the British economy.
"Who knows what they might get from Labour? Do you expect tough decisions from people who refuse to answer any straight questions?" Clarke, the chancellor of the exchequer, asked.
But he said it was plain that Labour had announced it would have a budget in July if it won power because it intended to raise taxes -- something Brown has consistently denied.
Clarke mocked Brown for having promised to keep current income tax rates while maintaining the levels of public spending the Conservatives have proposed for the next two years.
"Gordon, you can put on a Liverpool football shirt if you want, but it won't make you Robbie Fowler," he joked. "You can put on a mini-skirt, but it won't make you a Spice Girl."
"The public should realise -- if you vote Labour, you won't get Conservative policies.

"If you vote Labour, you call a halt to tax-cutting, you vote for higher spending, you give more powers to the (trade) unions... voting Labour means an end to the economic reform agenda which has transformed Britain from basket-case to role model," Clarke said.

He said there was a danger that Britain, which has had healthy growth and falling unemployment for the past three years, had developed such a successful economy that some people believed it would now be safe to have the first Labour government since 1979.
"They think now the Tories have got it right, Britain can take a holiday from history under Labour, and somehow put reality on hold," he said.

"If people vote Labour to escape from reality, they will soon have their illusions shattered. The fact is that the world has become a place of constant change... there is no turning back," Clarke added.
A poll in the Indepedent newspaper was gloomy reading for the Conservative faithful in Bath. It showed the party's support at just 27 percent against 52 percent for Labour.
